summary: Learners aged 11–13 distinguish the chemical meaning of 'pure' (a single element or compound with nothing else in it) from the everyday advertising sense ('natural/unadulterated'), and use melting/boiling behaviour as a purity test: at a given pressure a pure substance melts/boils at one sharp fixed temperature, while a mixture typically melts/boils over a range and at shifted values. The core activity is an empirical heating-curve comparison where learners observe the contrast rather than being told the rule; supporting activities add particle-level contrast, meaning-of-'pure' reference work, and categorisation/graph-reading practice. Formulations (deliberately designed useful mixtures such as paint, medicines, alloys) are previewed as a bridge to later (KS4) study.
misconceptions: 'Pure' means natural/healthy/unprocessed rather than a single substance.
A mixture and a compound are the same because both contain more than one element.
Adding salt to water raises its freezing point / doesn't change its boiling point.
Pure and impure samples melt at the same temperature.

activities.title: Purity tester: reading heating curves of pure vs impure samples
steps: Heat a sample of ice made from distilled water, stirring it, and watch a temperature-vs-time graph: observe that it stays roughly flat at about 0°C (at normal air pressure) while it melts, then climbs once it has fully melted.

Beside it, heat frozen salt water and observe that it starts melting below 0°C and that its temperature creeps up while it melts, instead of holding at one clean plateau. The exact temperatures depend on how salty the water is.

State in your own words what the SHAPE of each curve shows: one sharp flat step suggests a pure substance; a sloped spread across a range suggests a mixture (a useful rule at this level, although a few special mixtures can also change state sharply).
Take a 'mystery sample' round: given unknown heating curves, judge whether each sample is pure or a mixture and give your reason from the curve shape.

As a bonus, heat salty water next to pure water under the same conditions and compare. The salty water starts boiling at a slightly higher temperature (usually only about a degree, even with a lot of salt), and its temperature keeps creeping up as water boils away and the solution gets saltier. This shows that impurities both shift AND spread the transition.
activities.insight: A thermometer can act as a purity detector: at a given pressure a pure substance changes state at a single sharp fixed temperature, while a mixture usually changes state over a range and at shifted values — so melting/boiling behaviour is a test for purity, not just a property to memorise.

activities.title: Chemistry 'pure' vs supermarket 'pure'
steps: Examine an everyday label such as '100% pure orange juice — all natural' and decide whether a chemist would call it pure.
Compare a tap-to-reveal contrast of pure-substance and mixture particle pictures alongside annotated sharp-vs-range curves.
Write a sentence distinguishing the two meanings: everyday 'pure' = natural/nothing added; chemical 'pure' = a single element or compound with nothing else in it.
Classify examples: spring water (a mixture), distilled water (pure), salty water (a mixture that still looks clear).
activities.insight: The scientific meaning of 'pure' differs sharply from everyday use: orange juice and spring water are mixtures even though adverts call them 'pure', because scientifically 'pure' means a single substance only.

activities.title: Formulations: why we deliberately make mixtures
steps: List everyday designed mixtures — medicines, alloys, paints, fuels — and identify what useful job each component does.
Explain in a sentence why a 'formulation' (a mixture made to a precise composition) is deliberately not pure.

Discuss that the substances in a mixture are not chemically joined, so each keeps its own chemical identity and the mixture can in principle be separated by physical means, even though the mixture as a whole can have useful properties that its separate components lack (for example, an alloy is often harder than the pure metal).
activities.insight: Not all useful materials are pure: many are formulations — mixtures designed to a precise recipe so each ingredient contributes a needed property. Purity is desirable for identification, but mixtures are often what we actually want.

activities.title: Categorise and read: checking purity from evidence
steps: Sort given samples as pure substance or mixture, justifying each choice from composition or thermal behaviour rather than appearance.
Match heating curves to 'pure' or 'mixture' labels.
Read a melting point from a graph and state whether the sharp-vs-range shape indicates purity.
Explain whether pure water counts as a pure substance even though it is made of two elements, and why.
activities.insight: Purity can be judged from composition and thermal behaviour — not from how a sample looks — and a compound such as water is still a pure substance because it is one substance throughout.

checkQuestion: A carton says '100% pure orange juice — all natural.' In science, would a chemist call orange juice 'pure'? Then the important part: explain what 'pure' means to a scientist, and how you could TEST whether a clear liquid is pure or not.
checkAnswer: No — to a scientist orange juice is a MIXTURE (water, sugars, acids, pulp…), not pure. 'Pure' scientifically means a SINGLE substance (one element or one compound) with nothing else in it. You test purity by melting/boiling point: a pure substance melts/boils at a single sharp, fixed temperature, while a mixture melts/boils over a RANGE. Full marks need the everyday-vs-scientific distinction PLUS the sharp-melting-point test.
